title: Islamic Tabular Calendar Astronomical Epoch
intro: A mathematical Islamic lunar calendar that counts months using a fixed arithmetic scheme and an astronomical-era starting convention.
summary: Twelve lunar months, usually alternating 30 and 29 days, with leap-year adjustments. It is not a calendar of actual crescent sightings.
origin: The Islamic Hijri era begins in the seventh century. This particular tabular variant uses the astronomical Thursday epoch rather than the Friday civil epoch.
structure: A year has twelve lunar months. The arithmetic follows a repeating pattern and leap-cycle rules rather than observing each new moon.
pattern_note: The last month may gain a day in leap years. The asterisk denotes a length subject to the leap-cycle rule.
history: Tabular Islamic calendars permit date calculations into the past and future without requiring a published observation. Other Hijri calendars may differ by a day or more.
example: A computed date called 1 Muharram starts a new Hijri year in this model. An observation-based calendar can place the corresponding month boundary differently.
limits: The Thursday astronomical epoch is different from the Islamic Civil variant. Tabular values are not guarantees of a locally sighted moon or a particular authority's religious date.
